title: Tuning superconducting pairing symmetry via a staggered potential in the doped honeycomb Hubbard model
authors: Yanmei Cai, Yicheng Xiong, Ying Liang, Tianxing Ma
abstract: The ability to control superconducting pairing symmetry is crucial for designing unconventional and topological superconductors, yet practical tuning parameters beyond chemical doping remain limited. In this study, we investigate the effect of a tunable sublattice staggered potential on the pairing symmetry in the doped honeycomb Hubbard model. Determinant quantum Monte Carlo at finite temperature and constrained-path quantum Monte Carlo at zero temperature are employed to compute spin susceptibilities and pairing correlations in different channels. We find that increasing the staggered potential suppresses antiferromagnetic fluctuations and, at low doping, induces a transition in the dominant pairing tendency from $d+id$-wave to $f_n$-wave, with consistent results from both quantum Monte Carlo methods. In contrast, at higher doping levels, the system remains dominated by $d+id$-wave pairing even under an enhanced staggered potential. Moreover, strengthening the on-site interaction $U$ enhances the dominant pairing channel, underscoring the essential role of electronic correlations. Our results establish the staggered potential as a practical band-engineering tool for selecting unconventional pairing symmetries without varying the doping concentration, providing inspiration for designing graphene-based artificial superconductors and related doped band insulators such as Li${}_x$MNCl.
summary: This work investigates how a tunable staggered sublattice potential ($\Delta_0$) controls the superconducting pairing symmetry in the doped honeycomb Hubbard model. Using advanced Quantum Monte Carlo simulations, the authors demonstrate that $\Delta_0$ can drive a transition from $d+id$-wave to $f_n$-wave pairing at low doping. This provides a powerful theoretical blueprint for engineering unconventional superconductors without altering the material's chemical composition.
main_problem: The study addresses the challenge of controlling superconducting pairing symmetry in unconventional superconductors using tunable parameters beyond simple chemical doping.
main_result: Applying a staggered sublattice potential ($\Delta_0$) can induce a phase transition, switching the dominant superconducting pairing symmetry from $d+id$-wave to $f_n$-wave at low doping levels. This establishes $\Delta_0$ as a practical band-engineering tool for material design.
method: The research employs advanced quantum Monte Carlo techniques (DQMC and CPMC) alongside Cluster Mean-Field Theory calculations to probe pairing correlations in the Hubbard model.
model_or_system: The system modeled is the doped honeycomb Hubbard model, whose Hamiltonian includes hopping ($t$), on-site interactions ($U$), chemical potential ($\mu$), and a tunable staggered sublattice potential ($\Delta_0$).
key_observables: Pairing correlation functions (for $d+id$-wave and $f_n$-wave), spin susceptibilities ($\chi(q)$), and effective pairing susceptibilities ($	ext{P}_{	ext{eff}}$).
important_parameters: Staggered potential ($\Delta_0$), doping level ($\langle n angle$), and on-site interaction strength ($U$).
main_assumptions: The calculations rely on sophisticated numerical methods like DQMC/CPMC, and while comparisons with ED benchmarks are made, finite-size effects remain a consideration.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the phase diagrams showing symmetry transitions (e.g., $d+id$ to $f_n$) as $\Delta_0$ is varied at fixed doping, and show how pairing vertices depend on both $\Delta_0$ and $U$.
paper_structure: The paper systematically analyzes the effect of varying $\Delta_0$ across different doping regimes using multiple QMC methods. It first establishes the role of $\Delta_0$ in suppressing magnetic fluctuations, then details the symmetry transition at low doping, contrasts this with high-doping behavior, and finally confirms the correlation dependence via $U$.
why_interesting: The ability to tune superconducting pairing symmetries using an artificial potential (band engineering) is highly relevant for designing novel quantum materials and understanding exotic superconductivity mechanisms.
